title: Microfluidic Platform with Multiplexed Electronic Detection for Spatial Tracking of Particles
protocol: Design a set of four 7-bit Gold codes for encoding microfluidic channels.
Construct two linear feedback shift-registers, each representing a primitive polynomial.
Generate a preferred pair of 7-bit m-sequences using the LFSRs.
Cyclically shift the preferred pair of m-sequences and add them in mod 2 to generate four distinct Gold codes.
Design the layout of the coding electrodes.
Place three electrode terminals at three corners for positive, negative, and reference electrodes.
Route positive and negative electrode traces on opposite sides of each microfluidic channel.
Extend positive and negative electrodes into the microfluidic channels as electrode fingers following uniquely assigned Gold code.
Place the reference electrode in between the positive and negative electrode fingers.
Place positive and negative electrode traces far from the outermost reference electrode fingers to minimize electrical conduction outside the coding region.
Clean a 4-inch borosilicate glass wafer in piranha solution at 120 °C for 20 min.
Place the cleaned wafer on a 200 °C hot plate for 20 min to remove residual water.
Transfer the wafer to a spinner.
Dispense 2 mL negative photoresist onto the wafer.
Spin the wafer at a speed of 3,000 rpm for 40 s.
Place the wafer on a 150 °C hot plate and bake for 1 min.
Expose the photoresist to 365-nm UV light (225 mJ/cm²) through a chrome mask using a mask aligner.
Place the wafer on a 100 °C hot plate and bake for 1 min.
Immerse the wafer in RD6 developer for 15 s.
Gently spray deionized water to wash the wafer.
Dry by blowing compressed nitrogen.
Place the wafer with patterned photoresist into an e-beam metal evaporator.
Deposit a 20-nm-thick chrome film onto the wafer at a base pressure of 3×10^-6 Torr.
Deposit an 80-nm-thick gold film onto the wafer at a base pressure of 3×10^-6 Torr.

Immerse the metal-coated wafer into acetone in an ultrasonic bath set at a frequency of 40 kHz with 100% amplitude for 30 min at room temperature to etch the underlying photoresist and complete the lift-off process.
Dice the wafer into smaller pieces using a conventional dicing saw.
Spin the wafer at 500 rpm for 15 s.
Spin the wafer at 1,000 rpm for 15 s.
Spin the wafer at 3,000 rpm for 60 s to obtain a uniformly coated 15-µm thick photoresist layer.
Place the wafer face up on a cleanroom wipe soaked in acetone and remove the residual photoresist from the backside and edges of the wafer.
Transfer the wafer onto a hot plate for soft baking.
Bake the wafer at 65 °C for 1 min.
Move the wafer quickly to a 95 °C hot plate and bake for 2 min.
Expose the photoresist to 365-nm UV light (180 mJ/cm²) through a chrome mask by using a mask aligner.
Bake the wafer following exposure at 65 °C for 1 min.
Bake the wafer at 95 °C for 2 min.
Immerse the wafer in developer and gently shake the container for 3 min.
Rinse the wafer with isopropanol alcohol (IPA) and dry it by blowing compressed nitrogen.
If a white-colored residue appears on the wafer, immerse it into the developer again and develop for longer time and dry.
Bake the wafer on a 200 °C hot plate for 30 min to dry it completely.
Measure the thickness of the patterned photoresist using a profilometer at different locations across the wafer to ensure uniformity.
Add 200 µL of trichlorosilane in a Petri dish and place in a vacuum desiccator along with the SU-8 mold wafer for 8 h.
Place the 4-inch silicon wafer with the mold in a 150-mm diameter Petri dish.
Fix the Petri dish containing the silicon wafer by taping from its edges.
Mix polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) pre-polymer and cross-linker at a ratio of 10:1.
Pour 50 g of the PDMS mixture into the Petri dish.
Place the Petri dish in a vacuum desiccator to degas the mixture for 1 hour.
Cure the degassed PDMS mixture in an oven at 65 °C for at least 4 hours.
Cut out the cured PDMS layer using a scalpel.
Peel off the cured PDMS layer from the mold wafer using tweezers.
Punch holes with a diameter of 1.5 mm through the PDMS for inlet and outlet of the microfluidic channel using a biopsy puncher.
Clean the patterned side of the PDMS part by placing it on clean-room adhesive tape.
Clean the glass substrate with surface electrodes by rinsing it with acetone, IPA, DI water, and drying with compressed nitrogen.
Activate the surfaces of PDMS and glass substrate in oxygen plasma for 30 seconds using an RF plasma generator set at 100 mW.
Align the PDMS microfluidic channel with surface electrodes on the glass substrate using an optical microscope.
Bring the two plasma-activated surfaces into physical contact.
Bake the device on a 70 °C hot plate for 5 minutes, with the glass side facing the hot plate.
Connect the contact pads of the electrodes with wires by soldering.
Culture HeyA8 human ovarian cancer cells in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin in a 5% CO2 atmosphere at 37 °C until they reach 80% confluence.
Aspirate the media from the culture flask using a glass pipette.
Dispense and aspirate 1x phosphate buffered saline (PBS) to wash the cells.
Incubate cells in 2 mL of 0.05% (w/v) trypsin solution for 2 min at 37 °C to suspend adherent cells.
Add 4 mL of culture media to neutralize the trypsin.
Centrifuge the cell suspension at 100 × g for 5 min to pellet the cells in a test tube.
Aspirate supernatant completely.
Re-suspend the cells in 1-2 mL of 1x PBS by gently pipetting up and down to mechanically dissociate cell clumps.
Draw a small amount of cell suspension into a pipette.
Count the number of cells using a hemocytometer.
Dilute the cell suspension with PBS to prepare a sample with a final cell concentration of 105-106 cells/mL.
Place the Microfluidic CODES device on the stage of an optical microscope.
Apply a 400 kHz sine wave to the reference electrode on the chip using an electronic function generator.
Connect positive and negative sensing electrodes to two independent trans-impedance amplifiers.
Convert current signals from each electrode to voltage signals.
Subtract the positive sensing electrode voltage signal from the negative sensing electrode voltage signal using a differential voltage amplifier.
Use a high-speed camera to optically record operation of the device for validation and characterization purposes.
Drive the cell suspension through the Microfluidic CODES device at a constant flow rate (50-1,000 µL/h) using a syringe pump.
Measure the impedance modulation signal using a lock-in amplifier.
Connect the reference AC signal to the reference input of the lock-in amplifier.
Connect the differential bipolar signal to the lock-in amplifier as input signal.
Obtain the RMS amplitude of the differential signal from the lock-in amplifier output.
Sample the lock-in amplifier output signal at 1 MHz rate into a computer through a data acquisition board for further analysis.
Transfer recorded electrical data into MATLAB for post-processing and decoding.
Filter the recorded signal in the digital domain using a Butterworth filter to remove high frequency noise (>2.5 kHz).
Generate a template code library from sensor signals.
Identify representative non-overlapping code signals corresponding to each sensor in the device.
Extract these signal blocks from the dataset as separate waveform vectors.
Normalize each template code waveform vector by its power.
Measure the signal power using MATLAB's built-in function (bandpower).
Expand the template library using MATLAB’s (resample) function to create versions of normalized code signals with varying durations.
Identify signal blocks corresponding to sensor activity with an SNR threshold greater than 12 dB in the filtered waveform.
Treat waveforms with an SNR below the threshold as noise.
Use an iterative algorithm based on successive interference cancellation to decode individual blocks of sensor activity in the recorded signal.
Calculate cross-correlation of each signal block with all templates using sliding dot product.
Identify the template producing the largest auto-correlation peak.
Record the time and amplitude of the autocorrelation peak.
Construct an estimate of the sensor code signal by scaling the identified code template based on the measured peak amplitude and timing information.
Subtract the estimated sensor code signal from the original data.
Iterate the process until the residual signal does not resemble any signal in the template library, defined as a correlation coefficient less than 0.5.
Refine initial sensor signal estimations using an optimization process.
Reconstruct the signal by adding estimated individual sensor signals from each iteration.
Sweep the amplitude, duration and timing of individual sensor signals around the original estimates to produce the best fit with the recorded electrical signal based on least-squares approximation.
Convert amplitudes of estimated sensor signals into cell size by calibrating electrical signals against optical images.
